source_read: PDF, pp. 1-7 (article 102680; all pages; Tables 1-4 checked on pages rendered at 150 dpi, Fig. 1 at 300 dpi)

claims.overstatement: None in the Zaychik sentence: 'no detectable change' with the recomputed intervals is the correct reading, and the author's own conclusion (reform did not improve data) overstates. Qualifiers the claim could add: two of the seven earlier systems already used physicians (Massachusetts physician coroner, New Hampshire appointed physician) and two used justices of the peace, so 'replaced coroners' is approximate; the outcome is not a clean share (Table 3 numerator codes E869/E866.9 are missing from the denominator, consistent with the four unexplained shares above 1.00); standard errors appear unclustered, so 10-14 points is a minimum for what cannot be excluded; Fig. 1 shows pairs moving in opposite directions (New Jersey against New York, Massachusetts against Pennsylvania).
claims.note: Checked on rendered pages: seven treatment states 1976-1996 after dropping Delaware and Florida (1970); seven matched controls chosen by proximity and pre-trends; DID -0.02 (0.04), -0.03 (0.05), -0.02 (0.06); intercept 0.50-0.53; data 1968-1998, underlying cause only, all solid/liquid poisonings. Editors' intervals recomputed: -0.0984 to 0.0584, -0.128 to 0.068, -0.1376 to 0.0976, matching -0.10 to 0.06, -0.13 to 0.07, -0.14 to 0.10. The author states no comparable longitudinal drug-death study existed, supporting 'the one study'. Zaychik also reports, second-hand, the Warner et al. 92%/71%/73%/62% figures and a Maryland 85% undetermined figure (different year from the claim's 68%). Minor: 14 states x 31 years - 4 removed = 430, Table 4 says N = 429.

anchors.extracted: Medical examiners are usually appointed physicians and often forensic pathologists; coroners are often elected lay people with limited educational requirements and varying required training (author citing the 2009 National Academies report). The claim cites Goldberger et al. (2013) for the same point.

Second-hand (Warner et al., 2013): drugs specified on 92% of death certificates in centralized medical-examiner states, 71% in decentralized medical-examiner states, 73% in hybrid states and 62% in coroner states.

Author: the claim that coroners produce less accurate drug-death data rests on cross-sectional data alone; longitudinal evidence exists only for suicide; no similar longitudinal analysis had been done for drug-related deaths.

Difference-in-differences on CDC Compressed Mortality Files (county-level underlying cause of death; ICD-8 1968-1978, ICD-9 1979-1998). Table 1: nine states switched to medical-examiner systems: Delaware and Florida 1970, West Virginia, Arizona and New Mexico 1976, New Jersey 1978, Massachusetts 1983, New Hampshire 1986, Alaska 1996. Previous systems: justices of the peace (Florida, West Virginia, Arizona), coroner (New Mexico, New Jersey), physician coroner (Massachusetts), locally appointed physician (New Hampshire), magistrate coroner (Alaska), coroner with state ME (Delaware).

anchors.locator: 2. Materials and methods › 3rd-6th paragraphs; Table 2; Table 3
anchors.extracted: Controls from states that stayed coroner or mixed, chosen by geographic proximity and approximately parallel pre-switch trends in the nonspecific share over the prior decade; Delaware and Florida dropped (two pre-switch years), leaving seven pairs (New Hampshire-Ohio, New Mexico-Idaho, New Jersey-New York, Massachusetts-Pennsylvania, Arizona-Nevada, West Virginia-Indiana, Alaska-Montana). ICD-8/9 cannot separate drug overdoses, so all solid/liquid poisonings were used; outcome = nonspecific poisoning deaths (u) / all solid/liquid poisoning deaths (t); multiple-cause data exist only from 1999. Four state-years with u/t above 1.00 were removed; the author says this is unexplained because all nonspecific codes are in the denominator, but Table 3 lists E869 (ICD-8) and E866.9 (ICD-9), accidental poisoning by unspecified solid/liquid substances, in u and not among the t codes (E850-E859 / E850-E858, E950.x, E980.x), which would allow shares above 1.

Model: share = b0 + b1 after-switch + b2 treatment group + b3 after x group; three runs: all 31 years; 7 years before and 10 after; 7 before and 5 after (the latter two preferred by the author). No clustering of standard errors by state is described.

Both groups' nonspecific shares dropped sharply at the ICD-9 changeover (1979), giving significant negative 'year' coefficients; the DID interaction was negative, small (2-3%) and not significant in any model; author: little can be said about any effect of system change on specificity.

DID effect -0.02 (SE 0.04; N 429), -0.03 (0.05; N 236), -0.02 (0.06; N 176); intercepts 0.53 (0.02), 0.50 (0.03), 0.50 (0.03), i.e. a nonspecific share near one half; residual SE 0.19-0.20 on 425/232/172 df. Editors' 95% intervals recomputed (estimate +/- 1.96 SE): -0.10 to 0.06, -0.13 to 0.07, -0.14 to 0.10. The SEs appear to be ordinary least squares on state-years, so true intervals are probably wider.

Pairs diverge: after New Jersey's 1978 switch its nonspecific share stayed about 0.4-0.55 while New York's fell to about 0.1; Massachusetts fell below 0.1 while Pennsylvania rose to about 0.55; New Mexico and West Virginia fell more than their controls; Arizona and Nevada moved together; Alaska has two post-switch years. No state-specific estimates are reported, so the pooled null may average opposite changes.

Author concludes that reforming death-certification governance did not result in improved drug-mortality data, a stronger statement than non-significant estimates allow; the claim's 'no detectable change' is the accurate reading.

Explanations offered: ICD-8/9 coding differs from the ICD-10 used in cross-sectional studies; the system-quality link may be indirect (autopsy facilities, board-certified pathologists); antecedent factors (population density, political culture) may make the cross-sectional association spurious; staff and facilities may carry over, so some transitions may be 'empty title changes'; selection, since states that switched already resembled medical-examiner states; many modern coroners are forensic pathologists.

Anecdotes: after Montgomery County, Pennsylvania, elected a board-certified forensic pathologist as coroner (2007), use of the unspecified-drug code T50.9 in drug deaths fell by over 60 percentage points within two years; a similar drop in Franklin, Ohio, after a forensic pathologist was elected in 2008. Author suggests the official's qualifications matter more than the system label.

Second-hand (Warner et al.): Maryland listed 85% of drug deaths as undetermined intent against 1-30% in most states, attributed by the author to state classification policy rather than difficulty; New Mexico: 88.8% of 2013-2017 drug poisoning deaths carry T50.9 but only 2.9% carry it alone. The Maryland figure differs from the claim's 68% in 2016 (Slavova et al., 2019, as cited) because the source year differs.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-I, serious, driven by confounding (no fixed effects; the 1979 ICD-9 change falls inside 5 of 7 windows, checked) and by outcome measurement.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: the Discussion and Conclusion treat non-significance as no effect.
